_: Per-word teaching notes for the vocabulary module. HAND-AUTHORED — this is the one file here that is not generated, which is why it is separate from vocab-data-v1.json. build-vocab-data.py merges it in; regenerating never overwrites it.
_shape: Same four fields as the grammar module's lesson `exp` blocks — what / build / when / watch — so the two modules teach in one voice. `watch` is always the L1-interference trap, never a general caution.
_status: AI-AUTHORED, NOT REVIEWED. Every claim below is about Japanese and none has been checked by a native speaker. Goes to the reviewer with the rest of the queue. See the 'Reviewer — vocabulary module teaching notes' tracker row.
_scope: 13 of 89 taught words. Deliberately NOT all of them: the other 76 are plain nouns whose entire lesson is the gloss, and manufacturing a note for each would produce 76 shallow paragraphs that dilute the ones worth reading. A word earns a note when it carries something the gloss cannot say.

一緒に.what: The dictionary says "together," but 一緒 on its own is a noun — roughly "one and the same group." The に is what turns it into a description of HOW something is done, which is why the phrase is almost always 一緒に and not 一緒.
一緒に.build: 一緒に goes before the verb: 一緒に行きます. The person you are with is marked separately with と — 友達と一緒に行きます.
一緒に.when: Doing something jointly. Inviting someone, or describing an outing you shared.
一緒に.watch: English says "with my friend" once and is done, so learners write 友達一緒に or 一緒に友達. Japanese needs both pieces: と marks the companion, 一緒に says the action was shared. You can drop 一緒に and keep just と — 友達と行きます is perfectly natural and slightly plainer. What you cannot do is drop the と.

手を洗う.what: This is a phrase, not a word — 手 (hands), を (marks them as what gets acted on), 洗う (wash). It sits in the vocabulary list as a lump because that is how you will use it.
手を洗う.build: Keep を between them. Adding a topic goes in front and changes nothing else: 私は手を洗います.
手を洗う.when: Before eating, coming home, cooking. It is one of the small daily-routine phrases.
手を洗う.watch: Memorised as a single lump, it becomes hard to take apart later — learners who only know 手を洗う often stall on 手が汚い or 手が大きい, because they never registered 手 as a word in its own right. It is one word plus one particle plus one verb, and each piece works elsewhere.

歯をみがく.what: Same shape as 手を洗う: 歯 (teeth), を, みがく (polish, scrub).
歯をみがく.build: 歯をみがきます in polite form.
歯をみがく.when: Daily routine, usually alongside 起きる and 寝る.
歯をみがく.watch: みがく means polish or scrub, not "brush" — it is also what you do to shoes and to a skill. Translating it as "brush" hides that, and then 技を磨く looks like a different word.

薬を飲む.what: Medicine plus 飲む. Japanese takes medicine by "drinking" it, whatever its actual form.
薬を飲む.when: Any medicine — tablets, capsules, powder, liquid.
薬を飲む.watch: English "take medicine" tempts 薬を取る, which means physically picking it up. 飲む is the verb even for a tablet you swallow whole.

写真を撮る.what: Photo plus 撮る, a verb used specifically for capturing images.
写真を撮る.build: 写真を撮ります. The thing photographed takes の — 犬の写真を撮る.
写真を撮る.watch: 取る and 撮る are both とる and learners reach for the common one. 取る is take or pick up; 撮る is reserved for photographing and filming. Same sound, different character, and the checker will notice.

雨が降る.what: Rain plus 降る (to fall). Japanese makes the rain the thing doing the falling, so it takes が.
雨が降る.build: 雨が降ります. Past: 雨が降りました.
雨が降る.when: Describing weather that is happening or happened.
雨が降る.watch: There is no "it" in Japanese weather — 雨が降る is literally "rain falls." Learners looking for a subject to match English "it's raining" invent one. Also 降る is for things falling from the sky specifically; a dropped cup uses 落ちる.

勉強する.what: 勉強 is a noun — "study." する turns nouns into verbs, and a large part of Japanese vocabulary works this way.
勉強する.build: Two patterns are both correct: 日本語を勉強する, or 日本語の勉強をする. The first is more common in speech.
勉強する.when: Any studying. The same する trick makes 散歩する, 電話する, 料理する.
勉強する.watch: Mixing the two patterns produces 日本語を勉強をする, with two を in one clause — a very common early error and one the checker flags. Pick one shape and finish it.

散歩する.what: 散歩 (a walk, as a noun) plus する.
散歩する.build: 散歩します, or 散歩をします. Where you walk takes を in a different sense — 公園を散歩する, where を marks the space moved through.
散歩する.when: A walk taken for its own sake, not walking to get somewhere.
散歩する.watch: 公園を散歩する uses を on a place, which contradicts the "を marks the object" rule learners have just been taught. It is a real second use of を — the path or space traversed — and it turns up again with 道を歩く and 橋を渡る.

今日.what: Today. The reading きょう belongs to the whole word.
今日.build: Used like a noun. It usually needs no particle for time — 今日行きます, not 今日に行きます.
今日.when: Constantly. It is among the first words worth knowing cold.
今日.watch: きょう cannot be built from 今 (いま/こん) and 日 (ひ/にち). This is a word whose reading was assigned to the pair, so learn the sound as a unit. Taking it apart produces confident nonsense like いまび.

昨日.what: Yesterday, read きのう — again a reading that belongs to the whole word.
昨日.build: Like 今日, no particle needed for the time itself: 昨日食べました.
昨日.when: Talking about the past, usually with a past-form verb.
昨日.watch: Same trap as 今日. Also, 昨日 has a second, stiffer reading さくじつ used in news and formal writing — you will hear it, but きのう is what you say.

入る.build: Despite ending in -いる, this is a Godan verb: 入ります, 入って, 入った.
入る.when: Going into a room, a bath, a club, a company.
入る.watch: Verbs ending -いる or -える are usually Ichidan, and learners generalise the rule to produce 入て or 入ました. 入る is one of the well-known exceptions that is Godan anyway. So is 帰る. The ending tells you the likely answer, not the certain one.

帰る.what: To go home, or to return to where you belong. Read かえる.
帰る.build: Godan despite the -える ending: 帰ります, 帰って, 帰った.
帰る.when: Going home, going back to your own country.
帰る.watch: Two traps at once. It is Godan, not Ichidan (see 入る). And it means returning to your own place, so you cannot use it for going back to a shop or a friend's house — that is 戻る.

行く.build: Godan, but its て-form is irregular: 行って, not 行いて. Past is 行った.
行く.when: Everywhere. Pairs with に or へ for destination — 学校に行きます.
行く.watch: 行く is the one Godan verb whose て-form breaks the pattern, and it is common enough that the wrong form gets a lot of practice before anyone corrects it. Learn 行って early and separately.
